info.title: Nex Controller and Core API
info.description: Implemented development API for administrator inventory, enrollment, durable operations, appliance adoption and managed-VM creation. Capability-gated storage/network registration, bounded ISO transfer and stopped-VM provisioning use outbound authenticated Core reports. Browser VM consoles use single-use tickets, an outbound host tunnel and a same-origin WebSocket. Central VM power requests (start, shutdown, reboot, force-stop, force-reboot) are durable host operations. Controller-hosted qnetd witness candidate and certificate-registration routes are implemented for Core; two-host SBD arming and witness-loss promotion proof remain withheld.

get.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Read-only; safe to retry. Returns CSRF token for same-origin mutations. All authenticated administrator operations have controller-wide scope. Does not extend the idle deadline. A 401 requires sign-in again; session JSON fields are unchanged and contain no expiry timestamps.

post.summary: Sign in as administrator
post.description: Validates existing administrator credentials and browser origin. Sets __Host-nex_session with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/ and no Domain. Each login creates a new session; at most 64 active sessions per service. Sessions expire after 30 minutes without an authenticated mutation and eight hours absolutely; GET/HEAD polling does not renew them. Legacy unprefixed cookies are not accepted; sign in again after upgrade. Existing password hashes remain valid; new administrator bootstrap passwords must be nonempty valid UTF-8, at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes, without CR, LF or NUL; there is no minimum length or complexity rule. Login admission permits at most five valid-length attempts per one-minute actual peer-IP window, two concurrent password checks per service, and 4096 tracked peers. Forwarded client-IP headers are ignored. Login returns 429 when rate/concurrency/table or 64-session capacity is exhausted; bounded retries must not create an unbounded loop.

get.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Read-only; safe to retry. Pools are never created by administrators: each enrolling Core host becomes the master of a new pool named after its hostname (master_host_id). Membership itself is owned by the pool master: this list and POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members relay and display it, and the Controller never authorizes or persists membership intent of its own. The Core local API keeps the same authenticated member join flow as a host-local recovery path. Master change and member eject remain unavailable. Results represent persisted controller state.

get.summary: Show the pool master's reported membership and convergence
get.description: Administrator session. Read-only projection of what the pool master reports: its inventory.managed.membership, each member's connection freshness, its four convergence checks (pool-storage-reconciliation, pool-network-reconciliation, pool-media-reconciliation, pool-authority-replica) and counts of the master's member_access rows that are healthy, pending, failed or stale. It stores nothing and computes no membership of its own. authoritative is true only while the master's connection is fresh; when it is not, status, error, checks, access counts, failures, maintenance and maintenance_since are reported as unknown, null or empty rather than presenting the last mirror as current, and the client must show them as unknown. peer_origin is part of the master's durable record rather than an observation of it and is reported either way. Each member also carries its own reported staged join, its own reported guest list (known false when that host is not fresh), the newest pool-maintenance operation this Controller holds for it, and the authority replica as the member and the master each report it. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

400.description: Missing or invalid pool ID ("pool required").

post.summary: Add an enrolled host to this pool
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller makes exactly two calls and drives nothing: it asks the pool master for a single-use join invitation over one report round trip (pool_requests/pool_results, 45-second deadline), then hands that invitation to the joining host as one durable pool-join command. The joining Core performs the whole peer exchange with the master itself and reports progress as inventory.managed.join; a Controller that is lost after the command changes nothing about the outcome. The Controller validates only what it can see (pool and host exist, both fresh and not revoked, the joining host is the master of its own single-host pool with no managed VMs and no non-local storage, peer_origin is a bare https origin); every refusal that matters is still the master's and is relayed verbatim. master_url is an optional override that the web UI never sends: the master's own reported peer_origin wins when it has one; otherwise Core records the supplied master_url, or when none is supplied the origin it works out itself (https://<its default-route source address>:9444), as the master's own peer_origin the first time it issues an invitation. The joining host is handed the master_url from the invitation. Persist request_id before sending: an identical retry returns the original operation with 200 and never starts a second join, while the same request_id with any changed field (master_url included) conflicts. The invitation and pool CA are never returned, listed, logged or audited; the stored command is scrubbed of them as soon as the operation leaves queued and unconditionally 15 minutes after issue. Joining is not one-way: a member can be ejected with DELETE /api/v1/pools/{id}/members/{host_id}, the pool master can be changed with POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/master, and a surviving member can be promoted with POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/master/promote when the master is lost. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

Controller-visible refusals: "this host already belongs to the selected pool", "pool master must be fresh and active before a host can join", "the joining host must be fresh and active", "only the master of its own single-host pool can join another pool", "joining a pool with managed VMs is not supported; migrate or remove workloads first", "joining a pool with existing remote storage is not supported; detach it first", "the joining host must belong to the same site as the target pool", "pool request is already active", "request_id already used with another payload" and "request_id already used for another operation". A refusal the master itself decided is relayed verbatim in the same shape. A failed master result that carries no message becomes "the pool master refused to issue a join invitation", so a terse Core refusal is never an empty body.

No command was created and no membership changed; retrying with the same request_id is safe.

post.summary: Drain a pool member, or take it out of maintenance
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable pool-maintenance command to the pool master, which owns the flag inside the membership record it already keeps; the Controller records no drain of its own and the command is never sent to the host being drained. Maintenance refuses new VM placement, definition and start admission on that host and skips it in autostart; it stops no running guest and never blocks stop, shutdown or force-stop, so there is nothing to confirm and no confirmation field. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from host reports: the master is fresh and active, it has reported a membership, the host is a non-ejected member of it, and expected_version matches what it last reported. Core checks every one of them again against its own record, and its refusals arrive as a failed operation with conflict marked in GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/members, not as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

Also the shared idempotency refusals "request_id already used with another payload" and "request_id already used for another operation". Nothing was queued.

post.summary: Probe a host's local API TLS certificate
post.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Performs an insecure TLS 1.3 handshake to the given address (default port 9443) purely to capture the leaf certificate nex-core-local presents; it establishes no trust and stores nothing. This never contacts the Controller-to-Core enrollment contract; it only inspects the host's existing local API listener.

post.summary: Add a host by address and root password
post.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Replaces manual token enrollment for a reachable host: the operator first confirms the certificate fingerprint returned by probeHost, then submits it here alongside the host's root password. The Controller re-verifies that same fingerprint with a constant-time comparison during its own outbound TLS handshake to the host — a mismatch fails the handshake and returns 502 before the password is ever sent. On a verified connection the Controller signs in to the host's local API (POST /api/local/v1/session), mints a fresh site-bound enrollment token (the same token contract createEnrollmentToken uses), and pushes it to the host's local enrollment endpoint together with the Controller's own served HTTPS certificate (the -tls-cert file, not the host-identity CA) as the trust the host pins for its Controller connection; the host then enrolls with this Controller through the existing agent-enrollment contract and becomes the master of a new pool in this site. The root password is used once for that single sign-in and is never stored, logged, or echoed back, including in error messages. Unknown site_id returns 400. Optional host_id re-enrolls a revoked host whose pool belongs to this site (409 otherwise, checked before any network attempt). A wrong password returns 401; a login rate limit returns 429 with the host's own message. If the host reports it is already enrolled under a different identity, this returns 409 with that host_id — retrying the same add-host call after a lost response is safe and resolves the same way: fetch inventory to see the enrolled host. Any other host-side failure returns 502 naming the controller_url the host was asked to reach, and any token minted for the attempt is deleted. If the Controller process has no served certificate configured, 503 is returned before any host contact; use manual enrollment. One host-side enrollment refusal is a normal wait rather than a failure and is answered as such: a host that relays this Controller's own "pool identity is held; the pool master has not reported this ready member" gets 409 with retryable true and the host's own words preserved in host_error, not the 502 every other host-side failure keeps. It happens while a pool member is added to a replacement Controller before its pool master has reported it; connect the master first, or retry once it has reported the member.

get.summary: Read a host's management network and any change in flight
get.description: Administrator session required. Every field is a host report or this Controller's own operation history: the host's durable record (stage, spec, rollback deadline and time remaining), its reported interface inventory, its management-network health check and the newest management-network operation. The Controller stores none of it, so a replacement Controller returns the same answer as soon as the host reports. While the host is not fresh, state is "unknown" and check is null, but the record itself is still returned so a running rollback deadline stays visible instead of reading as success or failure. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

post.summary: Stage, apply, confirm or cancel a host's management network change
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable management-network command per step to the host, which renders, applies, times and rolls back its own configuration; the Controller computes nothing and keeps no copy of the change. stage writes nothing into /etc. apply swaps the three rendered files and bounces the management bridge, and starts the host's own rollback timer: unless a confirm arrives before the deadline, or if the host reboots first, the host restores the previous configuration by itself, with no Controller involved. confirm keeps the new configuration and is refused by Core until the host has observed its own connectivity over it. cancel discards a staged change, or immediately rolls back an applied, unconfirmed change. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from this host's reports; Core checks every one of them again, including the confirmation, which it alone can bind to itself, and its own refusals arrive as a failed operation rather than as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

post.summary: Enroll a Core host
post.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Outbound HTTPS; agent must verify Controller identity before transmitting its site-bound token. Provide a signed PEM ECDSA P-256 CSR and nonblank hostname (maximum 200 UTF-8 bytes, no CR/LF/NUL). Identity is host-owned: the host presents the host_id it generated and, as its pool's master, the pool_id and pool_name it keeps, and the Controller adopts them unchanged, so a replacement Controller recovers the pool with its original ID and name. host_id and pool_id must be canonical lowercase UUIDs (or the 64-hex form issued to hosts enrolled before host-owned identity) and pool_name a valid name, else 400. A fresh enrollment creates the pool in the token site with this host as its master, then records the host in that pool in the same transaction (audit pool.create and host.enroll); older agents that present no identity get Controller-minted IDs and a pool named after the hostname, which the response reports for the host to keep. A presented host_id already on record, or a pool_id already held by another master host, is 409: only a token bound to a revoked host may re-issue that host, and it must present that host and its pool (409 otherwise). A separate authenticated Core-local peer flow can subsequently join a member; this enrollment endpoint neither joins members nor changes master. The same key is the same host: a request whose CSR matches a recorded active credential (a retry after a lost response, even with a new token) returns that credential unchanged. Issues a 90-day host-specific client certificate and CA. The token binds to its first CSR; an identical token/CSR retry before token expiry returns the same identity without duplicate enrollment. A different CSR returns 409. After expiry or revocation obtain a new site-bound token; replacement requires explicit revoked host selection. Enrollment has no VM side effects. Compatibility: an older Controller rejects the new fields with 400 (unknown field); upgrade Controller and Core together.

post.description: Implemented in development product 0.4.11. Outbound host mutual TLS authenticates an enrolled host. Requires a fresh current pool master, and a reported membership matching pool_id/master/fencing_generation. post.summary: Report observations and reconcile commands
post.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0. Outbound mutual TLS authenticates exactly one enrolled, unrevoked host. Only report protocol version 1 is accepted and any other version is refused with 409; the first report starts repository negotiation without storage-repositories-v1, waits for the Controller storage_repositories acknowledgement, persists it, then advertises that capability. Clustered storage has its own v2 acknowledgement: a Core sends neither clustered results nor storage-clustered-iscsi-v2 until it receives storage_clusters_support with that exact capability. The Controller sends that acknowledgement on every preflight. A newly reconnected Core may offer the session-monitor preflight while withholding storage-clustered-iscsi-v2; before its acknowledged follow-up report, Controller clustered routes return retryable 503 negotiation pending without dispatching work or falling back. Core resets this readiness on start, Controller replacement/enrollment and report disconnect, so an older strict Controller sees only the clean preflight; queued Core results remain durable until a matching Controller acknowledges. Persist a strictly increasing sequence across restarts; discard superseded reports. Null/omitted inventory is heartbeat only and never makes old checks healthy. Results refer only to this host operations; acknowledge persisted results before deleting local journal entries. Commands can redeliver and must be reconciled by operation_id. Controller reconnect requires fresh inventory; no automatic VM restart is permitted. Sequence range is 1 through 9223372036854775807. Superseded sequences receive 200 but do not update last-seen or inventory; operation results and command redelivery still reconcile. At most 100 results per report; result error is at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes. Results for queued, undelivered operations return 409; known operation IDs belonging to another host return 400. Valid results for unknown operation IDs from a former Controller are acknowledged without creating operations or resource state. Terminal results are acknowledged without rewriting the original outcome, except an authoritative succeeded result for the same host and operation may settle a prior needs_attention outcome after Core recovery. At most 100 pending commands return, in creation order. Inventory fields merge only when inventory observed_at increases; individual checks merge only when their observed_at increases. Controller derives per-check freshness independently from heartbeat freshness. Health changes are recorded as debounced audit transitions (default debounce five seconds, configurable). Reports advertise at most 64 capabilities of up to 100 UTF-8 bytes each. managed-vm-v1 gates new commands; omission prevents managed delivery and a newer sequence clears stored capabilities. Result states include needs_attention for uncertain host effects. Automatic two-host BMC promotion reports the optional automatic=true flag in managed.transfer and managed.promotion; older Core versions omit it, and clients treat omission as false. A later authenticated terminal backup Result from the same host and operation ID can settle an earlier needs_attention Controller operation; backup inventory alone cannot, and cross-host Results remain rejected. After a Result is acknowledged, Core continues reporting the Controller-owned backup Journal outcome; a same-ID native vm-create cannot replace it, and peer-dispatched member work is excluded. Controller updates only its own matching nonterminal host/kind/operation row from this explicit outcome. Recurring backup metadata outcomes use the same rule; Controller adoption binds own operation and resource rows to the reporting host and kind before updating a nonterminal task, so colliding IDs from other hosts or kinds are mirrored separately.

post.description: Administrator session required. Mutations require same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token; JSON rejects unknown fields and bodies over 1 MiB. Persist request_id before sending. Identical payload replays return the same resource/operation; changed payload conflicts. New work requires a fresh active host in the selected pool advertising managed-vm-v1. Poll resource lists and operations for terminal results. HTTP acceptance is not host completion. Shared bounds, enforced identically on Controller and Core: 1–8 disks of 1–2048 GiB on virtio, sata or scsi with names unique in the VM; at most 8 NICs on virtio or e1000e with unicast lower-case manual MACs; at least 1 vCPU with sockets × cores × threads equal to the count when a topology is given; at least 512 MiB in memory mode dedicated or maximum; uefi or bios; boot orders unique and positive across disks and install media (gaps are allowed, since ejecting media leaves one), with at least one boot device. Controller additionally caps CPU at 64 and memory at 262144 MiB, assigns the UUID and refuses capacity above the host's observed CPU or memory. The host decides everything its own record answers: VM name and MAC uniqueness against its managed journal and libvirt domains, and dedicated-memory admission against total host memory, are reported as a failed vm-create result with the reason (visible in Task history), not as an HTTP refusal. Storage, network and ISO must have succeeded on this host and pool. The install ISO may be on any verified storage on that host; it need not share a repository with the VM disks. Core journals effects and reconciles per-disk ownership before replay; needs_attention preserves uncertain resources for manual recovery. start_after_create is honoured by the host inside the same creation: once the definition is verified the creation has succeeded, and Core starts the guest once, recording the outcome in the journal entry's start field so a retry never starts it twice. A failed automatic start keeps the VM as a normal stopped managed VM and is reported as a separate failed vm-power outcome (<operation-id>:start, 'VM created but not started: <reason>') in Task history; start it from the Power controls. autostart is a libvirt property set while the stopped VM is defined. No console, overwrite, automatic cleanup of ambiguous disks or guest installation. Core requires 2 GiB available host RAM reserve and verifies KVM/x86-64 and machine-type libvirt capabilities; uefi requires advertised EFI firmware. Failed/uncertain VM names remain reserved; there is no retry/deletion endpoint. A non-empty drivers_media_id requires the host to report vm-media-drivers-drive-v1 (409 "the selected host agent does not support a driver disc drive; upgrade Nex Core") and a succeeded ISO import on the same host and pool (404 "the driver disc ISO is not registered and verified on the selected host and pool"); both are checked after the replay check. Nonempty cpu.features requires vm-cpu-baseline-v1 after idempotent replay (409 on older Core). Core validates the explicit named CPU definition with native hypervisor-cpu-compare against the actual machine before creation/stopped edits/Core-mediated starts. Existing model-only definitions retain prior semantics; no guest-OS-specific CPU filtering. The 202 body may carry an optional warnings array. It is advisory and nothing else — the request was accepted, the pool master still decides, and every refusal, timeout and status is unchanged — and it names each required pool-shared repository, network or ISO whose access on the selected host this Controller's 30-second-old mirror does not show as current. The Controller deliberately does not veto on its mirror: that would make it a second placement authority and would refuse placements the master would accept. Nonempty tags require vm-tags-v1 on the selected host and its pool master after idempotent replay (409 on older Core).

post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The Controller validates pool/host scope then relays one bounded discovery request only to the addressed authenticated Core advertising storage-repositories-v1 and storage-discovery-v1. For kind iscsi, omit target_iqn to list targets with nonpersistent SendTargets; supply target_iqn to inspect only that target, requiring storage-iscsi-inspect-v1. Inspection uses Core's own initiator identity and an isolated read-only userspace connection, returns iscsi_luns with observed identities and per-LUN limitations, and never creates a kernel iSCSI session/node, mounts or formats a LUN, writes to storage, or changes existing sessions. Credentials travel only in the transient relay and private helper stdin, never command arguments or stored state. The Controller deletes its in-memory entry on delivery, result, browser cancellation or the 30-second deadline; Core work is bounded to eight seconds. Results contain no credentials, device paths, mount options or raw command output. A 200 observation may be empty or failed; 504 is stale when no Core result arrives before the deadline. Selected-target iSCSI inspection logs in as a second session using the host's own initiator IQN, so some single-session targets may reject or disturb it. The Controller validates every Core result (printable ASCII, bounded field lengths, at most 64 unique LUNs, LUNs only on a succeeded result) and treats an invalid result as failed. delete.summary: Remove a pool VLAN guest network
delete.description: Implemented in development product 0.3.5, protocol v1. Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required; JSON rejects unknown fields and bodies over 1 MiB. Controller only relays: the target host is always the pool master resolved from the pool record, so host_id is not accepted and a body carrying one is refused with 400 invalid JSON request. The pool master's Core checks the expected generation, refuses while any VM on any host in the pool references the network (running or stopped) and while any ready member's published VM inventory is stale, tears the guest bridge, its 802.1Q sub-interface when no other Nex stanza uses it and its /etc/network/interfaces.d stanza down, and journals a durable tombstone. Members converge on their next member pull pass, refusing locally while one of their own VMs uses the network. Only kind vlan networks are removable; a host-automatic bridge or libvirt network is refused with 409. 202 is acceptance, not teardown: the registration disappears from the library only when the master reports the tombstone. An identical request_id replays the same operation with 200; a different body under that request_id is 409. Two different answers share this route, decided by what the Controller already holds. On a registration whose operation failed and which no host reports as applied this is a local discard: it takes no body, relays nothing, deletes only the Controller's own request row, audits network.discard and answers 200 {"id", "deleted": true} — a refused registration published nothing on any host, so there is nothing to ask a host to undo. A failed row whose resource a host has since reported as applied is refused with 409 "a host reports this registration as applied, so it is not a failed request record; remove it on the host instead of discarding it". Everything above describes the relayed pool-VLAN removal, which is unchanged for a registration the master reports as applied. PATCH is unchanged too: a failed request record cannot be renamed.

put.summary: Replace a VM's definition on its assigned host
put.description: Implemented in development product 0.1.0, protocol v1. Requires an administrator session, same Origin and X-CSRF-Token. Persist request_id before sending; the same id replays the same durable operation, a different body under the same id is 409. The body is the complete desired definition (the same shape as creation); Controller validates its shape and references like creation, refuses immutable changes (an existing disk's storage, size or provisioning), and, when the VM is observed running, changes that need it stopped (name, CPU, memory, firmware, machine type, any boot order, an existing disk's bus, an existing interface's network, model, MAC or MTU, or adding a SATA disk); interfaces are matched by effective MAC: when the request names any current interface by its effective MAC (as the VM list reports it, and as the bundled editor sends every existing interface), every interface with an empty MAC is new; when it names none, an empty MAC is matched by position and the request is refused with 400 if it removes, reorders or changes an interface at an existing index, while an unchanged interface keeps the current address at its position. Clients that send any existing interface's MAC must send all of them, or an omitted one is replaced by a new interface. Controller freezes every automatic MAC into the definition before its stop-first check, drawing new ones from the VM's derived range at the first index above the highest one the current definition uses that no requested or current interface holds, or the lowest free index when none above is free, so a new interface never takes the address of one removed in the same edit, nor, unless the highest-index interface was removed or index 255 is in use, of one removed in an earlier edit; then it queues a vm-update command at revision current + 1 for the host's next report. Name and MAC uniqueness against other VMs and dedicated-memory admission are checked by the host against its journal and libvirt, as for creation. Core applies live what a running guest can take (adding or removing VirtIO/SCSI disks and interfaces, inserting, swapping or ejecting the ISO, description, guest OS hint and autostart) and redefines a shut-off guest from the regenerated XML; removed disks are detached and their files retained, never deleted. While validating a running guest's edit, before allocating any disk or changing any device, Core compares the live and persistent domains and reports the vm-update operation failed, changing nothing, with "network interface MAC <mac> is still attached to the running VM; wait for the guest to release it or stop the VM, then save again" when an added interface's MAC is still on a live interface that the guest has not released, changing nothing. The host reports the new definition as current and Controller refreshes its mirror from that report; poll operations for the result. One vm-update, vm-power or vm-media request per VM may be in flight. Nonempty cpu.features requires vm-cpu-baseline-v1 after idempotent replay (409 on older Core). Core validates the explicit named CPU definition with native hypervisor-cpu-compare against the actual machine before creation/stopped edits/Core-mediated starts. Existing model-only definitions retain prior semantics; no guest-OS-specific CPU filtering. Nonempty tags require vm-tags-v1 on the VM's host and its pool master after idempotent replay (409 on older Core); an edit that omits tags clears them.

post.summary: Change the pool master of a pool
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Hands the pool authority from the current pool master to a ready member of the same pool, keeping the pool, its networks, its storage registrations, its ISO library and its virtual machines with their identities and their names. While the change runs the pool master refuses every pool authority write — placements, definitions, start admission, joins, maintenance and pool resource registrations — with a message asking the operator to retry; nothing is queued behind it. Running guests are unaffected, stop and force-stop are never refused, and storage reservation releases are deliberately never frozen. This route has no automatic action: it is an operator request against a cooperating master. Core separately supports automatic promotion in eligible two-host pools using a recorded usable BMC fence profile with Host fencing enabled. The Controller relays exactly one durable pool-transfer command to the pool's current master and stores nothing else: no stage, no timer, no generation, no membership. Core runs the whole transfer by itself, so a Controller restarted, replaced or disconnected mid-transfer changes nothing and re-projects the transfer from the hosts' next reports. The refusals below are only what the Controller can already see from host reports; Core checks every one of them again against its own record, and its own refusals arrive as a failed operation with conflict marked in last_transfer of GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/members, not as an HTTP status here. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

Core refuses the eject while the host still owns any pool VM record or still holds a pool-shared storage reservation; those two refusals are deliberately not pre-checked here, because they are Core's decision, and they arrive on the operation. A member that is not reporting can be ejected: neither its freshness nor its capability list is gated, and it learns of the eject when it returns. The pool master cannot be ejected; change the pool master first. post.summary: Ask a surviving member what blocks its promotion
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. One brokered report round trip to the named promotion candidate (pool request action promotion-preflight): the candidate computes the whole verdict on Core from its own signed authority replica and its own live probes of the pool network, and the Controller mirrors the answer verbatim. Nothing is stored, journalled or audited and no command is issued, so this is safe to call repeatedly. The pool master is deliberately not required to be fresh, and its reachability from this Controller is never evidence in either direction: a preflight is exactly what an operator runs when the master is gone, and Core alone probes it. old-master-exclusion is normally unknown here, because Core fences and proves it during the promotion and never during a preflight; ready_to_fence, not can_promote, is the flag that says confirming now proceeds to the fence rather than to a refusal. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

Core's own sentence is relayed verbatim when the candidate answers failed; a failure with no text becomes "the promotion candidate could not compute a promotion verdict".

post.summary: Promote a surviving member after Nex Core fences the old pool master
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The operator action for a pool master that is gone. Exactly one durable pool-promote command is journaled, addressed to the candidate — the one pool command besides pool-join that does not go to the master, because the master is the host that is gone. confirmation is the pool's name, typed; fence_confirmed must be literally true and is the operator's separate acknowledgement that the old pool master will be powered off. Neither is evidence: Core produces and verifies the fence proof itself, no proof crosses the wire, and the acknowledgement is a precondition only. There is no expected_version, because the generation to check against is the dead master's and the candidate re-proves the whole verdict immediately before it activates. Nothing about the old master is pre-refused here — whether it answers, whether this Controller can reach it, when it was last seen — and neither is a missing or unusable fence profile, a lagging replica, a VM ownership conflict or a member holding a higher authority: all of those are Core's decision at run time and arrive asynchronously on the operation, surfaced verbatim in last_promotion. The Controller stores no verdict, fence proof, restriction, stage, candidate or generation, so a Controller restarted or replaced mid-promotion knows nothing about it until the hosts report and then re-projects it. This route remains an explicit manual promotion. Separately, Core supports a narrow automatic promotion for eligible two-host pools using a recorded BMC fence profile; it requires Host fencing enabled and does not use watchdog, storage lease or Nex Witness. The automatic path is owned and resumed by Core, not triggered by this route. No force, override, "declare host lost" or timeout-based path exists or may be added. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

An unknown host is forwarded rather than refused: the mirror is not the pool's record, and Core recomputes the whole set before it powers anything off.

post.summary: Record or clear how a member of this pool would be power-fenced
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. The profile is a field of the durable membership record the pool master owns, so this is the one promotion route relayed to the master and the one that needs a fresh one. One durable pool-fence-profile command is journaled; a null fence clears the profile. An optional credential is never stored by this Controller: it is handed to Core over the existing one-time encrypted credential handoff, Core allocates its own private reference, and only that opaque reference is written into the command — nothing reaches SQLite, the audit trail, the response or any log, and the stored replay payload is the profile as sent, so an exact retry stays byte-identical. Core then refuses asynchronously to record a profile whose material it does not hold, and refuses at record time any profile it could not verify. Recording a redfish profile is a live operation on Core: it connects to the controller, pins the certificate it presents, and proves the machine before the profile enters the membership, so an unreachable or wrong controller is refused now rather than during a promotion. Before any power-off Nex Core asks the management controller which machine it manages — IPMI Get System GUID, in either documented byte order, or the Redfish ComputerSystem.UUID — and compares it with the target host's own SMBIOS system UUID in the master's membership record. A mismatch, a missing recorded UUID and an unreadable controller each refuse the fence and power nothing off. A management controller is therefore recordable for a host that has reported its system UUID, which is how a physical pool is fenced; the virsh profile remains for a Nex Core running as a virtual machine in a disposable lab. Recording a usable profile for the pool master itself is what opts a pool into fence-verified promotion, and with it into the restart rule a restricted master follows. Implemented in development product 0.1.0.

post.summary: Detect how a member's management controller answers
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. One brokered report round trip to the pool master (pool request action bmc-probe), which probes the address itself — HTTPS Redfish and IPMI RMCP+ — from the host that would fence, and recommends a kind and system Id or plug. It takes the fence profile's gates: a fresh pool master whose reported membership includes the host. An optional password uses the one-time handoff with a probe-only bmc_probe purpose. Core removes both private credential copies after execution and expires an undelivered handoff after 10 minutes on its local probe tick or next startup. No discovery result or pool setting is stored, journalled or audited and no command is issued, so Detect is safe to repeat with a new request_id; recording the result is Set BMC access (POST .../fence-profile), which proves the controller again. The relay waits up to 3 minutes, because Core gives a probe up to 2 minutes and answers on its next report.

The host reads its system, CPU, memory modules, disks, PCI devices and temperature sensors on request and stores none of it; the Controller stores none of it either, so a replacement Controller sees the same report. A section whose source is missing or fails is returned unavailable with a reason and the rest of the report still returns. Serial numbers are returned to authenticated administrators only and are never logged. The report also carries system_disk: the disk the running system started from and the host's own record of its latest system disk replacement (see POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/system-disk), with the kernel's resync progress. post.summary: Rebuild a host's system disk onto a blank replacement disk
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable host-system-disk-replace command to the single host, whose own Core does the work and keeps the record: it revalidates the selected disk (the same identity, fingerprint and typed erase confirmation rules as the ZFS wizard, from the host's own storage discovery listing), refuses the disk the running system started from and a disk that holds data without the confirmation, lays the surviving disk's partition table on the replacement, copies the surviving disk's verified root slots, writes the boot partition and boot loader for the host's firmware (UEFI or BIOS) and adds the replacement to the nex-data mirror, which the kernel then resyncs. The host and its VMs keep running and nothing waits on the Controller. The Controller stores only the task it keeps for every host operation; the replacement's record and the resync progress come back in GET /api/v1/hosts/{id}/hardware (system_disk, md_arrays). request_id is the idempotency key: repeat it after a lost reply and the same operation is returned; after a failure, submit a new request_id and the host continues on the same disk without repeating a destructive step. Requires the host to be fresh, not revoked and to offer host-system-disk-replace-v1.

post.summary: Let a host configure its own management controller for fencing again
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Whether a host may configure its own management controller is a field of the durable membership record the pool master owns, so this is relayed to the master and takes the same membership and capability check a fence profile does. One durable pool-bmc-provisioning command is journaled for the master, which clears the host's bmc_provisioning_disabled flag and drops its last management-controller report; the host reads the decision from the pool records it already holds and creates the account on its next reconcile pass, because reporting a fence device before it exists would claim one that is not there. It is a desired state, not a transition: a host that is already allowed answers succeeded. There is no request to turn it off — clearing the host's fence device through POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members/{host_id}/fence-profile with a null fence is what withdraws a Core-provisioned device, removes the account from the controller and stops this host configuring it again, so one operator action has one meaning. Nex Controller stores nothing of its own: the decision lives in the master's membership and a fresh Controller recovers it from the master's reported inventory. Implemented in development product 0.4.2.

post.description: Queues backup-repository-register on the pool master. Administrator session, Origin, CSRF and a stable request_id are required. Core accepts NFS, SMB3, S3 and SFTP. The Controller accepts typed nonsecret SMB3, S3 and SFTP sources only with a matching one-time Core credential receipt that has been acknowledged. A failed first NFS/SMB3 mount start cleans Core's new unit so a fresh request can use the same ID after the service recovers; an uncertain cleanup is reported as a failure. Core forgets the repository and its recovery-point and run-history records and removes each host's mount and credential; destination data is never deleted, and registering the same destination again then rebuilding the catalog restores the recovery points. The command settles failed, changing nothing, while a backup job uses the repository, a backup, restore or test restore of it is pending or needs_attention (missed, skipped, succeeded and failed runs are history and are removed with it), a recovery point is pinned or reserved, retention or another metadata change on it is running, the name is wrong, or the counts changed. Core re-checks jobs, pins and counts after detaching the mount and records a removal intent, so a retry with the same request_id resumes a partial removal. post.summary: Ask a host to check, apply, activate, roll back, cancel, change its update source, scan media, import a bundle or fetch a payload
post.description: Administrator session, same HTTPS Origin and X-CSRF-Token required. Relays one durable host-image-update command to the single host, whose own update engine does the work (fetch and verify signed metadata, download with resume, write the unused slot, arm the next boot only on activate, return to the previous release when a boot fails) and keeps the record. The Controller holds no operation open and stores only the task it keeps for every host operation; progress, the staged and previous releases and the outcome come back in the host's inventory.image, and a refusal arrives as the failed task's error in the form "<code>: <message>" with the engine's stable code. request_id is also the host engine's idempotency key. The host-scoped settings, media, import and fetch actions are relayed the same way and are only asks: settings sets the host's channel and base URL (the host stores them in /etc/nex/updates.conf and reports them as inventory.image.base_url), media makes the host rescan its offline bundles (reported as inventory.image.media), import stages a release from a bundle on that host through the host's one verification pipeline, and fetch places an on_demand payload under /var/lib/nex/payload on that host. The Controller stores none of it. Pool rollout is not part of this route.
