nowayout.description: The kernel's setting that closing the device does not stop the timer. Where it is set, Nex Core cannot disarm this host without rebooting it, and reports that rather than resetting the host to get out of it.

in_use.description: Something already holds the device open, read from sysfs rather than by opening it.

PoolHostWatchdog.description: One host's own report of the watchdog device it has, read from sysfs on the host it is about and recorded by the pool master. A watchdog is how a host shuts itself out, so it has to have been reported while the host was alive. It is a slow-changing capability: it is written only when the finding changes and carries no timestamp, because nothing decides anything from how long ago a host last said it.

request_id.description: Stable client request ID. An exact retry answers with the same operation and never makes a second one.

enabled.description: The desired Host fencing state for the whole pool. A desired state, not a transition: re-sending the state the master already records answers succeeded.

PoolHostFencingRequest.description: Whether Nex Core may arm this pool's hosts to shut themselves out.

armed.description: Whether this host is feeding a watchdog that will reset it if it stops. A host that is not armed says why in detail.

kind.description: The device class this host armed. emulated is a device a hypervisor presents to a host that is itself a virtual machine: it really does reset that machine, so Nex Core arms it, and every proof and row resting on one says so because a hypervisor reset is not evidence about hardware. A physical host never reports it.

device.description: The sysfs device name sbd was given.

timeout_seconds.description: How long after sbd stops feeding the device this host resets. A watchdog exclusion proof needs at least twice this.

fencing_generation.description: The pool membership generation this host armed at. A watchdog exclusion proof is refused unless this is the generation being promoted, so a host that armed under an earlier record of the pool cannot be shut out on the strength of it.

detail.description: Nex Core's own sentence for why this host is not armed, or why it could not be disarmed cleanly.

feeding.description: Whether this host's watchdog device is still being fed, which is not the same question as armed. armed is what the pool may rest a proof on and goes false the moment the pool decides this host should stop; the device itself is released only when that host's cluster next stops, which can be a pass or two later. Every other host needs the difference: a host that leaves the pool's cluster while a peer is still feeding can take that peer below quorum, and that peer resets with nothing wrong.

observed_at.description: When this finding last changed, in the manner of PoolHostBMC.observed_at — not when it was last confirmed. Nothing decides anything from it: staleness is fencing_generation, which is durable and replicated and therefore still readable by a candidate whose master has gone.

armed_at.description: The host's own clock when it started feeding this device, carried over unchanged while it goes on feeding the same one. Nothing compares it with another host's clock. It exists so that a host which stopped and started its watchdog — a reboot, a cluster restart — produces a record that differs from the one before it: an identical record is never written and never replicated, and a survivor would otherwise be unable to tell "armed since before it left" from "was armed once, and has been up unarmed since". A survivor refuses a watchdog proof against a target that rejoined its Corosync partition after the last armed record it holds.

PoolWatchdogArmed.description: A host's own report that it has armed its watchdog, kept in the pool master's durable membership and replicated. It is the first of the three conditions of a watchdog exclusion proof, and the host that has to read it is a promotion candidate whose master has gone, which is why it is durable rather than an observation.

kind.description: The device class the target armed, copied from its armed report. emulated means the target is itself a virtual machine, so this proof is evidence about a hypervisor and not about hardware.

timeout_seconds.description: The target's own watchdog timeout, as its armed report gave it.

armed_generation.description: The pool membership generation the target armed at, which must be the generation being promoted.

held_seconds.description: How long this host has continuously been in a quorate partition without the target, on a monotonic clock. Any flap — the target reappearing, quorum lost, or this agent restarting — restarts it from zero.

bound_seconds.description: How long that had to hold: at least twice the target's own timeout, and never less than a minute.

partition.description: The hosts Corosync reports in this host's partition at the moment of the proof, by the pool's own votequorum. It must not name the target and must be more than one host.

PoolWatchdogExclusion.description: The whole evidence of a watchdog exclusion, one field per condition of the rule, so a proof can be read back later and judged rather than believed. Nobody performed this fence: the target reset itself, and the proving host only established that it must have.

PoolFenceCluster.description: The master's memory-only pool cluster observation. Pools of three to five ready hosts can form the watchdog cluster when Host fencing is on and no clustered-storage repository is configured. An eligible two-host pool instead can register Controller-hosted qnetd and configure Corosync qdevice; the reported forming/degraded status reflects qdevice state, but no two-host SBD arming or witness-loss exclusion proof is enabled. Durable witness selection and CA pin are in PoolMembership.witness; native readiness is rechecked after restart.

state.description: off is the pool's Host fencing setting. not_available means the pool has no applicable cluster or witness support. For the three-or-more-host watchdog cluster, forming waits for Corosync quorum, arming is the one-host-at-a-time rollout, and degraded means hosts are not all armed. In an eligible two-host pool, forming means qdevice or native quorum is not verified; it can coexist with an operating witness when Corosync is nonquorate. Degraded means the witness and quorum are operating but two-host watchdog arming remains withheld.

detail.description: Core's own sentence for the state. A client shows it as written.

witness.description: The pool master's current native qdevice observation, separate from watchdog arming. Omitted when no witness is selected.

armed.description: How many hosts of this pool's cluster are feeding a watchdog.

total.description: How many hosts are in this pool's cluster. Every ready host that is not in maintenance is in it: a host is never silently left out of the quorum the rest of the pool makes its decisions with.

arming_host_id.description: The host whose turn it is to arm, by host ID. Arming means restarting that host's cluster services, so exactly one host in a pool does it at a time, and whose turn it is is derived from the membership rather than granted. A host that cannot arm holds the turn and the rollout stops there with that host's own reason, which is the safe direction: fewer armed hosts is less protection, never a false proof.

MDMember.description: One dev-* entry of an md array: the partition, the slot it fills and the state the kernel reports for it.

name.description: Kernel name of the member partition, such as sda2.

slot.description: The array slot this member fills, or "none" for a spare or failed member.

state.description: The kernel's own member state, such as in_sync, spare, faulty or write_mostly; several are comma separated.

MDArray.description: One /sys/block/md*/md/ directory. A member the kernel no longer exposes is simply absent, so fewer members than raid_disks is how a failed disk appears.

level.description: RAID level as the kernel reports it, such as raid1.

raid_disks.description: How many members the array is defined to have.

degraded.description: How many members are missing or failed; 0 is a healthy array.

sync_action.description: The action the kernel is running: idle, resync, recover, check, repair or reshape.

sync_percent.description: Position in the running action, from md/sync_completed. Absent when the host reports none, so no progress is invented.

sync_speed_kbs.description: The kernel's current copy rate in KB/s while an action runs; absent when none does.

HardwareMDArrays.description: The Linux md arrays the kernel has assembled on this host, read straight from sysfs rather than parsed from mdadm. A host with no arrays reports an empty list, not an unavailable section. At most 32 arrays.

SystemDiskReplaceAccepted.description: Acceptance of the durable command. Acceptance is not the replacement: the host performs it when it collects the command and keeps its own record, which comes back as system_disk in GET /api/v1/hosts/{id}/hardware (the kernel's resync of the data mirror is in md_arrays).

SystemDiskReplaceRequest.description: The durable host-system-disk-replace command payload: one replacement disk for the system disk of the addressed host.

host_id.description: The host whose disks are replaced; the agent refuses a command addressed to another host.

request_id.description: The idempotency key: the host keeps its own record of the replacement under it, so a redelivered command replays the recorded outcome and never repeats a destructive step.
Stable per intent (8-64 letters, digits, - or _). Repeating it replays the same operation; a retry after a failed replacement uses a new one, which the host continues on the same disk.

device.description: One candidate of the host's own POST /api/v1/storage/discover listing with kind zfs-device: by_id, serial, size_bytes and fingerprint exactly as listed, and erase_confirmation equal to by_id when the listing marks the disk as holding old data.

HardwareSystemDisk.description: The host's own report on its system disk. State owner: Nex Core; the record is the host's, so a replacement Controller sees an operation another one started.

booted_disk.description: The whole disk the running system started from, such as /dev/sda. It is never a replacement target.

replacement.description: The latest system disk replacement this host recorded; absent when it never replaced one.

SystemDiskReplacement.description: Core's durable record of one system disk replacement, read from the host when asked for. The same record lets an interrupted replacement continue after Core restarts or the Controller is replaced.

by_id.description: The replacement disk's stable /dev/disk/by-id path as selected.

phase.description: accepted: checked, nothing written; laying: the partition table is written to the replacement; slots: the verified root slots are copied; boot: boot partition and boot loader; data: the replacement is added to the nex-data mirror; complete.

status.description: running also covers a replacement that Core's restart interrupted: it continues by itself.

error.description: Core's own sentence for a failed replacement; a refusal before anything was written ends with "this attempt changed nothing".

resync.description: The kernel's own progress of the nex-data mirror onto the replacement, present once the disk is a member of the array.

SystemDiskResync.description: What the kernel reports for the nex-data array and the replacement's member of it. percent is set only while an action runs, so an idle array has no invented progress.

array.description: Kernel name of the array, such as md127.

member.description: The replacement's partition in the array, such as sdb6.

state.description: The member's kernel state: spare while it waits, in_sync once the copy is complete, faulty if it failed.

action.description: The array's sync action, such as recover or idle.

percent.description: The kernel's position in the running action, in percent; null while none runs.

degraded.description: How many members the array is missing; 0 once the mirror is whole again.

PoolWitnessCandidate.description: A qnetd candidate advertised by the Controller. Current Core uses only the controller candidate: same-site pool-master candidates have no CA or pin and are not usable.

ca_pem.description: PEM CA certificate; empty for an unusable pool-master candidate.

ca_sha256.description: Lowercase SHA-256 of the CA certificate DER; empty for an unusable pool-master candidate.

PoolWitnessRegistrationRequest.description: Core registration request. cluster_name is the deterministic name for pool_id; fencing_generation binds credentials to the current pool fencing configuration.

PoolWitnessRegistration.description: Controller-signed qdevice credentials. address is empty for the Controller candidate; Core derives the qnetd address from its pinned Controller URL.

PoolWitnessRecord.description: The pool master's durable Controller qnetd selection and CA pin. Native readiness is re-established from Corosync and qdevice after restart; this record is replicated with pool authority.

PoolWrappedWitnessCredential.description: One host's native qdevice PKCS#12 credential, sealed to that host in its authority replica. It contains a shared qdevice key and is bound to the fencing generation.

PoolStorageLeaseConfig.description: Durable selection of the exact shared NFS repository used by the native sanlock storage-lease design. The feature is not available as an operator workflow and does not currently authorize automatic promotion.

PoolStorageLeaseExclusion.description: Native sanlock exclusion evidence shape. The corresponding two-host storage-lease proof path remains unavailable pending acceptance.

PoolVMSnapshot.description: Compact master-owned snapshot descriptor. Disk paths, XML and native artifacts remain in the owning Core journal.

BackupRepository.description: Master-owned backup destination record. Kinds are NFS, SMB3, S3 and SFTP; Core validates the kind and source.

source.description: Legacy NFS source; emitted for NFS records and omitted for other destination kinds.

credential_ref.description: Opaque Core-owned credential receipt reference; never credential material.

BackupRecoveryPoint.description: Master catalog index for one completed recovery point.

policy_id.description: Policy that created the point; retention prunes only that policy's points. Empty for manual backups.

BackupRun.description: Master-owned backup or restore run record.

capture_mode.description: Scheduled or run-now capture mode when present.

retention.description: Retention attached to a scheduled or run-now run when present.

host_id.description: Owner host of the backup or restore run when assigned.

manifest_sha256.description: Master catalog manifest digest pinned in a new restore run. Optional only for readable legacy runs; an unbound restore cannot execute or replay.

snapshot_id.description: Retained target ID for revert, distinct from the command operation ID; absent on create.

target.description: Exact master catalog descriptor resolved internally by Core for revert; absent on create and never supplied through the operator endpoint.

mode.description: Create capture mode. Omitted or stopped requires a shut-off guest. crash and quiesced require a running guest; quiesced also requires a responding guest agent. UEFI running capture is refused in this development slice.

ImageError.description: A stable refusal code with one literal message.

ImageRelease.description: One release on the host's A/B slots. root_hash is the dm-verity root hash; slot is a or b when known.

base_url.description: settings: the update server URL; empty clears it.

HostImageUpdateAccepted.description: Acceptance of the durable command. Acceptance is not the update: the host performs it when it collects the command; its engine's record comes back in inventory.image.

supported.description: True when the host offered image-update-v1.

image.description: Absent before the first acknowledged report.

host_id.description: The host whose engine runs the action; the agent refuses a command addressed to another host.

request_id.description: The host engine's idempotency key.

channel.description: settings (required): the channel to follow; import and fetch: the channel inside the bundle.

base_url.description: settings: the update server URL; empty clears it.

media.description: import (required) and fetch: a media id the host reported.

PoolUpdateHost.description: The master's record of one host's progress in a rollout. stage is the next unfinished step: pending, staged, teardown, drain, activate, boot, confirm, release, restart, soak, done or rolled_back. stopped_by_update lists the guests this rollout shut down on the host; it is written before the shutdown is requested, so a crash never loses which guests owe a restart. attempt counts how often the rollout has sent the host through staging again (a resume after a rollback); it is part of every step identity, so a new attempt is never a replay of the engine operations the earlier one left behind, and it is omitted while 0. retry_started_at is when the current run of guest shutdown or start failures began (omitted while unset).

retry_started_at.description: When the current run of guest-step failures on this host began; omitted while unset. The failure window is judged from here, so step_started_at and the six-hour step timeout are not restarted by it.

PoolUpdateRollout.description: The pool master's durable rollout record (pool-update.json beside pool-peer.json), replicated as the optional authority-replica section update_rollout (declared only while a record exists). A promoted master finds an active rollout paused with pause.code master_changed and an operator decides resume or abort. Hosts' own progress is in each host's state.json. Reported in Inventory.managed.update_rollout by the master only, withheld until the Controller acknowledges image-update-v1. id is the request_id that started it; finalized_sequence is set only once every host committed the release.

PoolUpdateControlResult.description: Core-owned replicated control receipt retained across later rollouts. Exact request_id/normalized intent replay returns the original snapshot or error; snapshots omit controls. No rollout and no code means an unresolved outcome, continued by Core without Controller. replication_pending also blocks competing transitions until the terminal result is acknowledged. At most one unresolved/ACK-pending receipt exists; it names the current rollout. Terminal records have no reservation; rollback_started is valid only for an unresolved rollback_host.

replication_pending.description: The immutable terminal result awaits the existing required authority ACK; Core retries acknowledgement before admitting another transition.

reserved_result_bytes.description: Reserved addressed-authority capacity for an unresolved result; included in all admission checks and released when its terminal snapshot/error is recorded.

rollback_started.description: Durable rollback intent retaining the original host attempt/step identity; it does not prove a replica ACK or host dispatch. Transport loss is reconciled under that unchanged identity.

PoolUpdateView.description: GET /api/v1/pools/{id}/updates: the master's own rollout record, projected from its last report. supported is true only when the master and every non-ejected member advertise pool-update-rollout-v1. The Controller stores nothing of it.

PoolUpdateAccepted.description: Acceptance of the durable pool-update command. Acceptance is not the rollout: the master performs it when it collects the command; its record comes back in Inventory.managed.update_rollout.

PoolUpdateStartRequest.description: Body of POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/updates/check and …/updates/rollouts. request_id becomes the rollout ID; an exact replay returns the same operation, the same request_id with another body is 409. running_vms: refuse (default), shutdown, or evacuate (refused evacuation_unavailable).

running_vms.description: refuse (default) waits for every guest to stop, then pauses naming them; shutdown gracefully shuts the host's guests down, records stopped_by_update and restarts them on the same host through master start admission; evacuate is refused evacuation_unavailable (live migration does not exist yet).

PoolUpdateControlRequest.description: Body of a rollout control. pause takes effect between hosts; resume rechecks membership; abort restores maintenance and stopped guests before completing; rollback_host arms an activated host's previous release while paused. Core durably binds request_id to normalized intent and replays its original result/error across rollouts and promotion; changed intent is request_conflict. A pending replica acknowledgement uses the same ID/body; a new action or retry after terminal refusal uses a new ID.

PoolUpdateRequest.description: Request of the update-rollout and update-control pool commands. sequence and running_vms (refuse waits for every guest to stop then pauses naming them; shutdown gracefully shuts the host's guests down, records stopped_by_update and restarts them on the same host through master start admission; evacuate is refused evacuation_unavailable) start a rollout; dry_run runs only the preflight; rollout_id, control (pause, resume, abort, rollback_host) and host_id address an existing one.

force.description: Only with control abort: end a pending abort cleanup (abort_cleanup_pending) without confirming it. Refused abort_not_pending when no abort is pending.

PoolUpdatePause.description: Why a rollout is paused. code is one of operator_paused, master_changed, needs_attention, running_vms, step_timeout, rolled_back, unconfirmed, quorum_margin, host_busy, ha_enabled, membership_changed, abort_cleanup_pending (an abort could not confirm that every started host was put back; resume and rollback_host are refused, abort retries or force ends it). needs_attention carries vm_inventory_unavailable, vm_shutdown_failed or vm_start_failed in its message after 5 minutes of failures.

PoolUpdateStep.description: One idempotent rollout step (peer step route). step_id is deterministic per (rollout, host, stage): a repeat is the same step and is answered from the host's current state, never run twice. Actions: check (verify the release is offered), stage (stage only; never arms the next boot), drain (gracefully shut down exactly vm_ids), activate (arm and reboot; the engine keeps its refuse policy), confirm, undrain (start exactly vm_ids through master start admission) and rollback.

PoolUpdateStepResult.description: done false with no code means still running: ask again with the same step_id. code is the host engine's stable refusal code.

PoolUpdateTarget.description: What a host verified about the release it was asked to install.

controller_image.description: The release is controller_first and carries a Controller image.

PoolUpdateHostStatus.description: One host's own read-only observation of its image engine and guests (peer status route).

controller_vm.description: This host runs a Controller appliance in the two-disk profile that it can swap.

ImageMedia.description: One offline update bundle the host found. Channels are read from the unverified channel.json for display; the host verifies everything on import.

PoolUpdateController.description: The controller_first step of a rollout. stage scan looks for the host that runs the Controller VM, swap waits for that host's journaled appliance swap, done means no Controller is left to update first. attempt is part of the swap's step identity (a resume after a failed swap is a new swap) and is omitted while 0; error is the code: message of the last failed swap.

BackupS3Source.description: S3-compatible HTTPS endpoint, bucket, optional prefix and signing region for a backup destination.

endpoint.description: HTTPS endpoint with verified TLS identity.

BackupSFTPSource.description: SFTP host, root path and pinned SSH host-key fingerprint for a backup destination.

BackupRemoteIdentity.description: Observed remote destination fingerprint used for S3 and SFTP identity checks.

BackupRepositoryHealthTransition.description: Historical repository health transition; not a fresh access result.

attention_count.description: Failed, missed or needs-attention runs in the unfiltered retained history.

BackupCatalogPage.description: At most 64 recovery points and 2 MiB of JSON. A changed generation requires restarting at the first page.

next_cursor.description: Decimal offset for the next page; omitted on the last page.

generation.description: SHA-256 of the complete unfiltered catalog; pass it with next_cursor.

total.description: Number of recovery points matching the current filters.

untested_count.description: Points without a passing restore test in the unfiltered retained catalog.

backup_days_14.description: UTC dates with backups in the latest 14 calendar days, across the unfiltered catalog.

OrphanCleanupRequest.description: Deletes the recovery points of the chosen VMs, which are not in the pool's VM inventory, from a repository's destination and catalog.

vm_ids.description: VMs chosen explicitly; there is no wildcard.

include_protected.description: Also delete protected points; otherwise they are skipped.

confirmation.description: 'delete N recovery points', or 'delete N recovery points including P protected' with include_protected.

recovery_points.description: Recovery points of the chosen VMs the operator was shown.

protected_points.description: How many of them are protected.

BackupOrphanGroup.description: One missing VM's recovery points in a repository.

vm_name.description: Name recorded by the newest point.

size_bytes.description: Sum of the sized points' disk and firmware artifacts.

size_unknown_points.description: Points the destination could not size within the query's budget.

in_use.description: A point is pinned by an unfinished restore or test restore, or a pending backup run names the VM; cleanup skips those points.

BackupOrphanQuery.description: A repository's recovery points whose VM id is not in the pool master's durable VM inventory.

warnings.description: Backup jobs that still list a VM missing from the pool.

BackupOrphanCleanup.description: The pool master's durable record of one orphaned-backup cleanup: the planned points and each one's outcome.

GET /appliance-ready.json.description: Appliance-only public JSON file served by the existing Controller UI file handler, not a separately registered API route. First boot atomically publishes it after initialization, verified local HTTPS UI HTTP 200, and guest bootstrap-secret cleanup. It must be absent from a pristine appliance image and may return 404 before preparation or on non-appliance deployments. A persisted marker records first-boot completion; it is not continuous health or successful host enrollment/adoption.
GET /appliance-ready.json.compatibility: Host handoff requires bootstrap_version 1, status ready and a successful UI root response over the pinned Controller TLS identity. An older API-only Controller cannot satisfy appliance readiness.

refresh-inventory.payload: None: only operation_id and kind. Created by POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/operations with a stable request_id; at most one queued or dispatched refresh per host.
refresh-inventory.semantics: Read-only request for a fresh host inventory sample. Core journals it as pending without a managed payload and completes it succeeded when a probe inventory observed after admission is reported, or failed with 'fresh host inventory unavailable before probe deadline'. A pending refresh restarts its deadline after agent restart so it reconciles against a new sample. Delivered without the managed capability. A repeated operation_id is ignored as already admitted, including for legacy journal entries without a stored command; no effects are repeated.

pool-member-join.semantics: Reserved master-directed pool command. Core refuses it because membership is admitted only through the authenticated one-use Core-peer exchange; Controller cannot create or replace membership.

pool-join.semantics: The one pool command addressed to the joining host rather than the master: its target is pool.member_host_id. Created by POST /api/v1/pools/{id}/members after the master answered the brokered invite. The joining Core runs the whole peer exchange itself, as a durable staged join persisted in its own Core state: precheck, csr, joined, rehomed, advertised, ready. Each stage is individually idempotent, so a crash, reboot or Controller outage resumes at the stage still to perform; the agent re-attempts it from its own loop with no Controller involvement, and reports progress as inventory.managed.join. The invitation and pool CA in the payload are single-use and short-lived; the Controller scrubs them from the stored command as soon as the operation leaves queued and unconditionally 15 minutes after issue. Core refuses the join outright when the host is not enrolled, holds managed VMs or non-local storage, is not the master of its own single-host pool, or is already a member; a host that is admitted but has not finished the remaining stages reports needs_attention and stays a member, never a silent success or a false failure. Ten failed attempts before any membership change end the operation failed rather than retrying an expired invitation forever.

pool-storage-reconcile.semantics: Master-directed reconciliation for one NFS or SMB repository. The addressed member pulls the master record over pinned TLS 1.3 peer mTLS, stores an SMB secret only in its own Core credential state, journals native preparation, verifies QEMU access and a cross-Core non-blocking lock, then posts its generation-bound access observation. Before member VM/media work it reserves the current repository generation at the master; failed local work releases that reservation, while a durable definition retains it until the healthy serialized member journal proves it unused. Master source/credential/detach mutations write a Core-owned marker and fail closed while reservations exist. Local ZFS, ordinary iSCSI and generic native disks remain local and are refused/no fencing applies. Controller does not authorize membership, receive SMB secret bytes, or drive retries.

peer_lock.security: Pinned TLS 1.3 mTLS; current authenticated pool member. POST checks repository eligibility and generation. Lease ownership is bound to the authenticated member, repository, generation, challenge and mode.

parameters.challenge: 32 hexadecimal characters, generated randomly per attempt
parameters.probe_mode: Optional challenge-byte-v1; absent means legacy byte zero

peer_lock.acknowledgement: 204; challenge-byte-v1 POST echoes X-Nex-Pool-Probe-Mode: challenge-byte-v1. Missing echo selects legacy byte zero; a different nonempty echo fails closed.
peer_lock.semantics: A nonzero one-byte OFD range derived from the challenge on .nex-peer-lock isolates simultaneous proofs. Only EAGAIN/EACCES establish conflict; after DELETE the member must acquire the same range. A rare range collision fails closed. Unknown modes and malformed challenges are rejected; unavailable generation or lock returns failure. Leases expire after ten seconds and are not VM ownership or fencing authority.
peer_lock.compatibility: New master supports legacy byte-zero requests. New member falls back to byte zero when an old master omits the acknowledgement, retaining the legacy contention limitation. Core retries periodically with a fresh challenge; no Controller retry job or new durable state.
peer_lock.offset: SHA-256 of decoded 16-byte challenge; big-endian uint64 of first eight digest bytes, AND ((1<<63)-2), then add one. Byte zero is reserved for legacy peers.

lease_limit.at_capacity: New leases return lock-unavailable conflict; exact held-lease replay remains idempotent. Release or ten-second expiry frees capacity.

storage-register.semantics: Verify existing local directory access; no formatting. Refuse, as a failed result, a path another non-failed registration on this host already holds. The host self-registers /var/lib/libvirt/images as ISO through this same verification, with a host-generated ID, unless any journal entry already holds that path. Succeeded registrations are reported back in Inventory.managed.storage and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-storage:<host>:<id>) without redelivery.

storage-zfs-provision.semantics: Master-directed durable ZFS provisioning. Core owns repository identity, validates stable selected devices immediately before destructive work, journals recovery and performs selected member work through authenticated Core-peer transport. Results are reported in Inventory.managed.zfs_provisions for adoption after Controller replacement.

storage-zfs-replace.semantics: Master-directed replacement of one failed leaf device of a provisioned ZFS pool. It is addressed to the pool master, which accepts it only for its own pool and only for a repository its own record already holds on the named host, and either performs it locally or forwards it to that ready current member over the authenticated Core-peer channel. The executing host revalidates the pool and the disk against a fresh observation, then runs wipefs --all on the replacement and zpool replace; the command is complete when zpool replace returns, and the resilver that follows is reported by the ordinary per-host ZFS observation. ZFS retires the old device itself when the resilver finishes; nothing detaches it. The host journals the operation under its state directory, keyed on operation_id: a redelivered command replays its recorded outcome, a pool already resilvering onto the replacement is adopted as success, an operation ID reused for a different repository, failed leaf or replacement is refused, and an agent interrupted after the wipe resumes from the wipe-started stage, where the wiped disk can no longer match its fingerprint and the identity that survives a wipe (the same by_id, serial and size) is checked instead. The master then records the replacement disk on its own repository record. Master-side refusals are failed results ("ZFS disk replacement targets another pool", "only the pool master may replace a ZFS disk", "this pool master has no ZFS repository of that ID on that host", "the selected ZFS host is not a ready current member"); the executing host's refusals arrive as needs_attention carrying its own sentence ("<device> is no longer part of this pool; check the pool before replacing a disk", "<device> is online, so there is nothing to replace", "the replacement disk cannot be safely observed", "the replacement disk changed since it was selected, or is in use", "the replacement disk holds old data and was not confirmed for erasure", "the replacement disk could not be cleared", "<old> could not be replaced with <new>").

storage-update.semantics: A name-only update is metadata-only and preserves credentials without reconnecting. Source changes and credential rotation are guarded: rotation requires all referring VMs shut off and no pending or needs_attention disk/media/ISO work. Core compares generation, journals intent before effects, reports needs_attention if rollback is uncertain, and never returns or journals credential bytes.

storage-recheck.semantics: Core observes the registered source without changing configuration or credentials. A missing, replaced, readonly or inaccessible backing source is reported and blocks future disk/media writes; it never uses an empty mountpoint. An identical Controller replay only returns the original operation. Core separately retries at most one due pending/needs_attention storage journal entry per minute in its serialized managed-worker lane, retaining the original result and excluding definitive failures; this continues through Controller loss.

storage-detach.semantics: Core compares expected generation and applies the full dependency guard for VM disks, retained disks, ISO media and pending/needs_attention disk or media work. A success writes a tombstone and removes only Nex-owned access configuration; it never formats, erases, destroys a zpool or target, or deletes backing files. Uncertain rollback remains needs_attention.

storage-credential-retire.semantics: Core rechecks that the opaque receipt is eligible and unreferenced before removing its local secret. A receipt already retired cannot restore or recreate a secret by replay. The command carries no credential bytes and Controller keeps no cleanup state.

network-register.semantics: Verify existing bridge or active libvirt network without edits; for kind vlan, idempotently create bridge <uplink>v<vlan> over the 802.1Q sub-interface, persist it under /etc/network/interfaces.d and refuse uplinks or VLAN devices already used by the host configuration. Refuse, as a failed result, a bridge (shared by kind bridge and vlan) or libvirt network another non-failed registration on this host already holds. The host self-registers <port> untagged for every bridge on a physical NIC or bond through this same verification, with host-generated IDs, unless any journal entry already holds that bridge. Succeeded registrations are reported back in Inventory.managed.networks and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-network:<host>:<id>) without redelivery.

network-remove.semantics: Remove a pool VLAN guest network (kind vlan only; anything else is the failed result "only pool VLAN networks can be removed"). Core checks the expected generation, then refuses while any VM definition on that host references the network, running or stopped ("network cannot be removed while used by VM <uuid>"). On the pool master the agent additionally refuses while any VM in any member's published inventory uses it ("… on host <host>"), and fails closed when membership or that inventory cannot be read or a ready member has not published at the current membership generation ("pool VM inventory is incomplete; wait for every member to report before removing this network"). Teardown proves ownership from the /etc/network/interfaces.d/nex-<bridge> stanza Nex itself wrote ("bridge <b> was not created by Nex; remove it by hand"), refuses a bridge carrying any port but its own guest port ("network still has attached interfaces"), deletes the bridge, deletes <uplink>.<vlan> only when it is a VLAN device with no master that no other Nex stanza names, and removes the stanza. The uplink, the management bridge, host addresses, routes and /etc/network/interfaces are never touched. Teardown is idempotent, so an interrupted removal settles on replay and there is no needs_attention outcome. Success journals a tombstone: the network leaves Inventory.managed.networks as a tombstone row, the host stops rebuilding the bridge, and the Core ID can never be re-registered — re-adding the same uplink and VLAN mints a new network with a new identity, so VM NICs must be re-pointed.

network-update.semantics: Rename a pool VLAN guest network. The payload carries no uplink, VLAN or source, and the projection copies only the name, so a rename structurally cannot re-plumb a bridge; kind, source, uplink and VLAN are unchanged and the single native effect is one atomic rewrite of the /etc/network/interfaces.d/nex-<bridge> stanza, whose header comment carries the name. The generation becomes expected_generation + 1. A member applies the master's name one generation at a time, so a member several renames behind steps through each one and never reports a generation it did not apply; a member whose journalled source, uplink or VLAN differs reports "pool network <id> changed uplink or VLAN; remove and re-add it" instead. A stale expected generation is refused with "network generation is no longer current; refresh and retry".

iso-import.semantics: Without media.url, fetch assigned staged media over host mTLS and verify supplied size/hash/ISO. With media.url, require iso-download-v1 and zero initial size/hash; Core downloads public HTTP(S) destinations with DNS/redirect address checks, no credentials or environment proxies, capacity limits and ISO validation. Core records computed size/hash in its durable applied journal, then reports Inventory.managed.media without URL. Controller mirrors completion metadata and a fresh Controller re-adopts identities and names. Interrupted dispatched work is reconciled through the journal; ambiguous imports require attention.

media-remove.semantics: Remove an imported ISO. Core checks the expected generation ("ISO generation is no longer current; refresh and retry"), refuses while any VM definition on that host names the ISO as media_id or drivers_media_id, running or stopped ("ISO cannot be removed while attached to VM <uuid>"), and on the pool master also refuses for any VM in a member's published inventory ("… on host <host>") and fails closed on incomplete member inventory. Teardown unlinks the published file <storage>/nex-media/<id>.iso and nothing else; a file already gone is success, which is also what the second host on shared storage observes. No VM disk is touched. Success journals a tombstone: the ISO leaves Inventory.managed.media as a tombstone row, and neither VM creation nor a member's shared-media adoption resolves it any more.

vm-create.semantics: Create a stopped VM from the full specification: one exclusive new qcow2 per disk inside the VM's own directory on each disk's storage target (sparse when thin, preallocated when not), one interface per NIC with its derived or manual MAC, per-device boot order, the memory mode's balloon and physical-backing configuration, the selected firmware and machine type, and libvirt autostart when requested. Refuse, as a failed result, a name another domain or non-failed journal entry on this host holds, an effective MAC (manual or derived) any domain or journal entry holds, and dedicated memory that, with what is already promised plus the 2 GiB host reserve, exceeds total host memory. When start_after_create is set, start the guest once after the definition is verified and record the outcome in the entry's start field; the creation result is succeeded either way. A retry or reconciliation never starts twice: an interruption at the start step is reconciled by observing libvirt (running means started, otherwise the start outcome reads 'interrupted before the automatic start completed'). A failed start keeps the VM defined and stopped and is reported as a separate outcome <operation-id>:start of kind vm-power, status failed, error 'VM created but not started: <reason>'. Reconcile journal and per-disk ownership on replay. Core resolves storage, network and media references by resource ID, not by pool/host ID, so creation works after re-enrollment under a new Controller. Succeeded definitions are reported back in Inventory.managed.vms and adopted by a Controller that does not hold them (request_id adopt-vm:<host>:<id>) without redelivery.

vm-power.semantics: Issue one libvirt start/shutdown/reboot/destroy/reset for the named VM on this host. start and force-stop are idempotent against the observed state; shutdown and reboot are ACPI requests the guest may ignore; force-reboot maps to virsh reset, is running-only, and shares reboot's interrupt ambiguity; paused or transitional states are refused. The stage is journaled before the single request so an interruption is reconciled by observation only: succeeded when the observed state proves the outcome, otherwise needs_attention; never a second request. Queue-capable hosts (vm-power-queue-v1) persist FIFO command admission and check after_operation_id is a successful same-VM task before effects; no retry loop for genuine failures. Host-received queued commands survive restart/replacement and are reported as managed outcomes for passive adoption. Shutdown/reboot completion remains ACPI acceptance, not proof of guest shutdown.

vm-delete.semantics: Undefine a stopped managed VM. Requires observed shut off. delete_disks=false retains qcow2 paths in the journal; delete_disks=true unlinks them after undefine. UEFI guests use virsh undefine --nvram. Succeeded deletes omit the VM from Applied.vms and emit DeletedVMs tombstones for Controller mirror removal. An interrupted undefine or wipe resumes when the same operation is delivered again: a domain still defined must be shut off (otherwise needs_attention 'stop the VM so its interrupted delete can finish; observed state is <state>'), undefine repeats with the same flags and a requested wipe repeats over the journaled paths, ignoring files already gone. A later vm-delete for the same VM settles the interrupted one only when delete_disks matches and then fails as already deleted; a different delete_disks choice is refused. Disks of a VM deleted with delete_disks=true no longer count as storage-detach dependencies.

vm-media.semantics: Insert a verified ISO into, or eject media from, the named VM's CD drive on this host with one libvirt change-media (live and persistent). Insert attaches an empty CD drive first when the domain has none; eject on a drive that is already empty (checked against the live definition of a running VM) succeeds without any libvirt call and never attaches a drive. The resolved media path and the changing-media stage are journaled in one write immediately before the change, so an interruption before that write is simply re-applied and one after it is reconciled by observing the domain: succeeded when the drive holds the requested media (or none, for eject), otherwise needs_attention. Core records only media_id in the VM's journaled specification; boot order values are never rewritten because change-media leaves every device's bootindex as it is.

vm-update.semantics: Apply one revision of an existing VM's definition; refuse a revision other than current + 1. Classify the difference from the journal's current definition (NeedsStop): a shut-off guest is redefined after any new disks are allocated and a rename (domrename), with the same capacity, name and MAC conflict checks as creation; a running guest takes only device additions, removals and media changes, applied with attach-device/detach-device --persistent and change-media --live --config, and is refused before any effect for anything else; an added interface whose MAC is still live after an earlier removal the guest has not released is refused and the task fails before any effect. Disks are matched by name and keep their journaled target names; interfaces by MAC. Removed disk files are retained and listed in the journal. The persistent definition and per-disk ownership are then observed against the regenerated XML by device identity; an interruption is reconciled by observation, except a UEFI-to-BIOS change interrupted after its undefine (stage cleaning-nvram or defining), which Core finishes by confirming the domain is absent and defining the journaled BIOS XML, and which refuses to undefine a UEFI domain that reappeared. A stopped edit that renames the VM and changes Secure Boot runs the read-only Secure Boot checks first, then domrename, then the variable-store edit and define. The journal reports the highest succeeded revision as the VM's current definition.

pool-maintenance.semantics: Addressed to the pool master, never to the host being drained: the master owns the membership record the flag lives in, and entering or leaving maintenance never contacts the drained host. Only membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, enabled and the optional expected_version are on the wire. The master sets PoolMember.Maintenance and MaintenanceSince in its own pool-peer.json and deliberately does not bump the membership generation, so draining a host cannot invalidate an in-flight placement, a published inventory or a peer generation check. enabled is a desired state, so re-sending it succeeds and leaves maintenance_since unmoved, which is what makes an exact retry after a lost reply safe. Core refusals are definite failed results: "only the pool master records maintenance mode", "no such member of this pool", "an ejected host has no maintenance state", "pool membership is unavailable", "pool membership changed since this request was composed; review the pool and try again", "maintenance command carries no maintenance request" and the PoolCommand.Valid() texts. A durable save that may not have landed is reported needs_attention with "maintenance mode could not be recorded durably"; the next inventory report states the truth and the exact retry is safe. While the flag is set the master refuses new placement, define and start admission for that host with "the selected VM host is in maintenance mode; take it out of maintenance before placing or starting VMs on it", and skips it in autostart-by-placement. It never blocks stop, shutdown or force-stop, never stops a running guest, never blocks local recovery and never blocks the member's own convergence.

management-network.semantics: Addressed to the host whose management network is being changed, and performed entirely by it. Two identities ride in the request: operation_id is the command envelope's own, unique per command, because it is the managed journal's replay key; change_id names the change Core acts on, which is the operation_id the host recorded when it staged it and reports back in inventory.management_network. stage validates and renders the spec, snapshots /etc/network/interfaces, /etc/dhcpcd.conf and /etc/resolv.conf and writes <state-dir>/management-network.json, touching nothing in /etc. apply records the applied stage and its deadline before any file is written, then renames the three rendered files into place and bounces br0; a failed write or a bridge that will not come up rolls back immediately. confirm keeps the change, clears the deadline, bumps the revision and drops the snapshot. cancel discards a staged change or rolls back an applied, unconfirmed change at the operator's request. The host rolls back by itself when the deadline passes and when it finds it rebooted after the apply, at agent start, on every probe tick and from an exact in-process timer; no Controller is involved. Core refusals are definite failed results. Conflicts end with "management network conflict": "a management network change is already applied and waiting to be confirmed or rolled back", "management network revision is <n>, not <m>", "no management network change is staged as <id>", "no management network change is applied as <id>", "management network change <id> is <stage>", "management network change <id> is <stage> and cannot be cancelled", "the rollback deadline for <id> has passed; the previous configuration is being restored", "this host has not yet been reached over an address of br0 itself under the new configuration; a Controller report that arrived over another interface, or a local API call from this machine, does not count", "the host network configuration changed since this edit was staged; stage it again". Plain failures are "management network command carries no request", "management network request does not match its command", "the confirmation does not name this host", "this host cannot read its own name to check the confirmation", the ManagementNetworkRequest.Valid() and spec validation texts, "rollback window must be between 2m0s and 30m0s", "<path> is not a regular file (<mode>); replace it with a plain file before changing the management network", "<path> is missing; Nex Core will not create a management network configuration it cannot prove it rendered" and "<path> was not written by Nex Core or the Nex installer; edit it from the host console instead". Guest VLAN bridges under /etc/network/interfaces.d are never read, written or brought down, and /etc/systemd/network/*.link is never rewritten, so interface renames are not part of a staged change. Re-staging the same change id with a different spec is refused with "management network change <id> is already staged with a different configuration": an exact retry replays the staged change, while the same id carrying another configuration is not a retry at all, and answering "succeeded" would report on the recorded change while the operator is looking at the one they just sent.
management-network.capability: management-network-v1 on the target host. The Controller offers no management network control without it.

pool-transfer.semantics: Addressed to the pool's current master, never to the subject host: the master owns the authority being moved, and it drives every step itself. action is master-change, eject or transfer-cancel; only membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, the action and the optional expected_version are on the wire. The master records a durable Transfer record in its own pool-peer.json before anything else happens and advances it on every tick, so the operation survives a Controller that is restarted, replaced or disconnected, and a power cycle of either host. Terminal results: succeeded; failed, which is a decision and means nothing moved; and needs_attention, which is not an error but "durable and still running — the hosts finish it". Core refusals include "only the pool master starts a master change or an eject", "no such member of this pool", "only a ready member with a peer endpoint can become the pool master", "another pool authority transfer is already in progress on this pool", "pool authority is frozen for a master change; retry when it completes", "pool authority was handed to another host; this host is no longer the pool master", "host <id> still owns pool VM records (<ids>); move or delete them before ejecting it", "host <id> still holds a pool-shared storage reservation on <repo>; let it finish before ejecting it", "no pool authority transfer is in progress on this pool", "the pool authority transfer in progress has another target" and "the target has already activated this pool authority; the master change can only go forward", "host <id> is already removed from this pool's membership; the eject can only go forward" and "this pool promotion has powered the old pool master off; it cannot be cancelled and can only go forward". A cancelled eject records "the pool member eject was cancelled by an operator"; a cancelled master change records "the pool master change was cancelled by an operator". A cancel is accepted only before the transfer's first irreversible durable step, and Core reports that answer itself as PoolTransferStatus.cancellable rather than leaving a caller to judge by stage name: a master change stays cancellable through freeze, replicate and activate, including the hand-off window, where it succeeds only if the target proves under its own lock that it never activated; an eject stays cancellable through freeze and remove, and is refused once the membership without that member has been written; a promotion is never cancellable, because it has powered a host off. The reported flag is computed from the same predicate the cancel is gated on, so the two cannot drift. While the transfer holds the freeze every pool authority write on the master is refused rather than queued; running guests keep running, stop is never refused and storage reservation releases are never frozen. Before a planned master change or eject records its first freeze, Core refuses unresolved backup journal work, pending backup runs and pending metadata receipts with "backup operation is unresolved; finish or reconcile it before changing pool authority"; the check and first durable freeze hold the same backup authority lock. Fenced promotion may inherit pending backup authority and reports those runs/receipts needs_attention, retaining restore pins instead of queuing their native work on the new master.

pool-promote.summary: Promote a surviving member to pool master after fencing the old one
pool-promote.target: The promotion candidate itself — the one pool command besides pool-join that is not addressed to the master, because the master is the host that is gone.
pool-promote.semantics: One durable, resumable machine keyed by operation_id, driven entirely on the candidate. Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: promote, member_host_id (the candidate), fence_confirmed: true, fence_host_ids}. fence_host_ids is the exact set of hosts the operator agreed to power off, as the verdict's fence_host_ids named them — the old pool master, and every other host that blocks the promotion and can be excluded by a fence. Core refuses without it ("this promotion will power off other hosts; confirm the hosts this pool reports before it can run") and compares it again at run time against the set it computes itself, so a pool that changed since the preflight stops the promotion rather than quietly fencing something new: "this promotion must power off <ids>, which is not what was confirmed; confirm the hosts this pool reports and try again" and "this promotion no longer needs to power off any host; review the pool and try again". A host is never powered off without having been named to the operator first. No membership travels: the candidate reads the signed replica it already holds. It moves nothing until Core has proved replica integrity, replica supremacy, accepted ownership and a fence proof Core itself produced — an independently observed power-off of the recorded fence target, digest-bound to this pool, this excluded host, this operation and this generation, and at most 15 minutes old. A returned fence agent status, a timeout, a missed heartbeat or an operator assurance cannot construct one. The whole verdict is re-proved immediately before activation, so a member that returned between the fence and the activation stops it; activation adopts VM ownership first, then makes this host master at generation + 1 in one atomic write, and an interrupted promotion resumes at the stage that did not complete. Terminal results: succeeded; failed, which is a decision and means nothing moved; and needs_attention, which is not an error but "durable and still running". Core's own refusals arrive on the operation and are surfaced verbatim in last_promotion: "the pool master <id> is reachable and holds this pool's authority; change the pool master with a planned master change instead of promoting", "the pool master <id> has no recorded fence profile; record one before promoting", "the pool master <id> has not been fenced for this promotion; Core fences it and observes the power-off when the promotion is confirmed", "this promotion has no fence proof for the old pool master", "this fence proof excludes another host", "this fence proof belongs to another promotion", "this fence proof is not bound to this promotion", "this fence proof is older than 15m0s; fence the old pool master again", "the old pool master was not excluded: <native reason>", "pool host <ids> holds a newer pool authority than this host; promote it instead", "pool VM <ids> is recorded differently by the host that owns it; resolve that before promoting", "this host holds no pool authority replica; it cannot be promoted", "this host's pool authority replica was never verified", "this host holds no fence credential for <host>; it cannot fence it, so it cannot be promoted over it", "the replicated fence credential is not addressed to this host", "the replicated fence credential is unreadable", "this host already holds different material under that fence credential reference", "this host is already the master of its pool", "promoting this host powers the old pool master off; confirm that before the promotion can run" and "a pool promotion is performed by the candidate itself". A cancel is never accepted: "this pool promotion has powered the old pool master off; it cannot be cancelled and can only go forward". This command is the manual promotion path. A separate Core-owned automatic path is limited to eligible two-host pools with Host fencing enabled and a recorded usable BMC profile; no automatic watchdog, storage lease or Nex Witness path exists. There is no election; no force, override, "declare host lost" or timeout-based path exists or may be added.

pool-fence-profile.summary: Record or clear how a member of this pool would be power-fenced
pool-fence-profile.target: The pool master, which owns the durable membership record the profile lives in.
pool-fence-profile.semantics: Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: fence-profile, membership.master_host_id, member_host_id, fence}. A null fence clears the profile. The profile is written into the master's durable membership and replicated with it, so a promoted master inherits it and a fresh Controller re-adopts it from the master's reported inventory. No credential material travels on this command: credential_ref names a file the existing one-time encrypted fence-credential handoff has already delivered to the master, and Core refuses to record a profile whose material it does not hold — "this host holds no fence credential for <host>; deliver it to this host before recording the profile" and "this host's fence credential material for <host> is larger than this pool replicates; shorten it before recording the profile". Core also refuses at record time any profile it could not verify, in the shape "this fence profile cannot be verified by this host: <reason>", releasing the delivered credential when it does: "this host does not report a unique hardware identity, so a management controller cannot be confirmed to be its own", "this management controller did not answer, so the machine behind it could not be identified", "this management controller rejected the recorded account, so the machine behind it could not be identified", "the management controller at this address reports a different machine than the host it is recorded for; nothing was powered off", "a management controller fence device needs the account Nex Core signs in with", "virsh fencing needs an immutable domain UUID target" and "SCSI persistent-reservation fencing is unsupported". Before any power-off Nex Core asks the management controller which machine it manages — IPMI Get System GUID, in either documented byte order, or the Redfish ComputerSystem.UUID — and compares it with the target host's own SMBIOS system UUID in the master's membership record. A mismatch, a missing recorded UUID and an unreadable controller each refuse the fence and power nothing off. Other refusals: "only the pool master records a fence profile", "no such member of this pool", "an ejected host has no fence profile". Recording a usable profile for the master itself is what opts a pool into fence-verified promotion, and therefore into the boot rule of a restarted master; clearing it is durable and is only released once every ready member has acknowledged a replica built without it.

pool-bmc-provisioning.summary: Let a host configure its own management controller for fencing again
pool-bmc-provisioning.target: The pool master, which owns the durable membership record this decision lives in.
pool-bmc-provisioning.semantics: Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: bmc-provisioning, membership.master_host_id, member_host_id}. It says one thing — this host may configure its own management controller again — and re-sending it is a success, because it is a desired state and not a transition. The master clears PoolMember.bmc_provisioning_disabled and the host's last management-controller report, and the host creates the account on its own next pass. The opposite direction is not a command: clearing a Core-provisioned fence profile sets the flag, removes the account and stops provisioning, in the one path that clears a profile. Refusals: "this command carries no management controller request", "only the pool master records whether a host configures its own management controller", "pool membership is unavailable", "no such member of this pool", and the authority-write refusals a fence profile takes while a master change is in flight.

pool-host-fencing.summary: Turn this pool's host fencing on or off
pool-host-fencing.target: The pool master, which owns the durable membership record this setting lives in.
pool-host-fencing.semantics: Payload: PoolCommand{request_id, action: host-fencing, membership.master_host_id, enabled}. It names no member, because the setting is the pool's. The master records PoolMembership.host_fencing_disabled as the negative of enabled and replicates it with the pool's records; every host reads it from the copy it already holds. It is a desired state and not a transition, so re-sending the state already recorded answers succeeded. Turning it on arms nothing by itself: Nex Core arms a host's watchdog only where every prerequisite in PoolFenceSummary.prerequisites holds, and the quorum line is unknown until this pool runs a quorum service. Refusals: "this command carries no host fencing request", "only the pool master records whether host fencing is on", "pool membership is unavailable", and the authority-write refusals a fence profile takes while a master change is in flight.

snapshot-create.semantics: Core-owned VM snapshot create. The local Core API accepts one stable snapshot operation ID, optional mode (omitted/stopped for shut-off guests; crash or quiesced for a running guest), and exact current VM definition, persists intent, obtains the current pool-master reservation, captures native disk and firmware recovery state, and settles the compact descriptor in the master catalog before reporting success. Quiesced mode requires a responding guest agent and does not silently downgrade; UEFI running capture is refused in this development slice. Same-ID exact replay returns the journaled result; changed intent, unknown outcome, unavailable authority or incomplete evidence remains refused/pending for reconciliation. Controller does not execute or schedule the operation.

snapshot-revert.semantics: Development stopped-revert slice under integration. Core resolves the retained target and captured specification, persists a distinct operation journal, obtains an exact target-bound master reservation, and must verify all disk/configuration and paired firmware effects before settlement. Revert preserves current VM identity/name/description/tags/autostart and increments its specification revision; it does not start the VM. Unknown effects remain fenced for exact-operation observation. Controller only adopts Core-reported outcomes.

snapshot-delete.semantics: Development stopped leaf-delete slice under integration. Core resolves the retained target, refuses points with native children before effects, persists a distinct operation journal, and obtains an exact target-bound master reservation. Current leaf delete uses public blockcommit without --delete, metadata-only snapshot-delete, reference scan, and unlink of proven-unreferenced overlays. Completed settlement removes the catalog entry without changing the VM specification. Exact retries past reservation must not repeat native effects. Controller only adopts Core-reported outcomes.

snapshot-metadata.semantics: Development catalog metadata update. Authenticated host-local PATCH updates only the pool master's retained name and description for an existing snapshot ID. Capture digests, creation time and disk identity stay fixed. Duplicate names and unresolved recovery reservations are refused. Later revert and delete bind the updated descriptor digest. Controller only adopts host-reported catalog rows.

backup-repository-register.semantics: Controller queues registration of an NFS, SMB3, S3 or SFTP backup destination on the pool master. Core owns the durable pool-backup-repositories.json record. Exact request_id replay is required; Controller stores no authoritative repository catalog.

backup-repository-test.semantics: Controller queues a mount/access check for a registered backup repository on the pool master. Core updates observed access; Controller only relays.

backup-repository-forget.semantics: Controller queues removal of a backup repository from the pool on the master. Core drops the repository, its recovery-point records and run history, and each host's credential and mount; it never deletes destination data. It refuses with a failed Result while a backup job uses the repository, a backup, restore or test restore of it is pending or needs_attention, a recovery point of it is pinned or reserved, another change to it is running, the typed name is wrong or the recovery point counts differ from the confirmed ones. Replays by request_id return the recorded Result; a repository that is already forgotten succeeds.

backup-now.semantics: Controller queues a stopped full backup of one VM into a registered repository. Client request_id is the Core operation ID. Core publishes a complete recovery point or refuses; Controller adopts outcomes and catalog rows from master inventory. An uncertain, already published manual backup without retention can settle on exact replay from a validated point even if the destination later refuses writes; a fresh backup still requires write access.

backup-restore-as-new.semantics: Controller queues restore-as-new on the selected host. Core copies validated artifacts locally first, then creates a new stopped VM. Controller never keeps an authoritative recovery catalog.

backup-test-verify.semantics: Controller queues operator verification of a test restore. Core records the result beside the catalog point; Controller adopts from master inventory.

backup-test-cleanup.semantics: Controller queues cleanup of one test restore VM and its staging only. Core removes that test guest; other recovery points are untouched.

backup-policy-upsert.semantics: Controller queues create/update of a master-owned backup policy. Core persists pool-backup-policies.json; exact request_id replay is required.

backup-policy-pause.semantics: Controller queues pause or resume of a backup policy on the pool master. Core owns enabled/paused state; Controller adopts inventory.

backup-policy-delete.semantics: Controller queues deletion of a backup policy definition on the pool master. Removes only the policy definition (schedule, VM list and retention rules) on the pool master, so no further runs are scheduled for it. Recovery points, run history and repository data are never deleted; retention no longer applies to the points the policy created, which stay restorable and removable through the recovery point flows. Refused (a failed Result, nothing changed) while any run of the policy is pending or needs_attention, or when the confirmation is not the policy name. Replays by request_id return the recorded Result; a policy that is already gone succeeds only for the request_id that deleted it.

backup-policy-run-now.semantics: Controller queues an immediate one-shot run of a backup policy for selected VMs. Core records occurrence IDs under pool-backup-runs/; Controller adopts outcomes.

host-image-update.semantics: Addressed to one host and performed entirely by its own update engine, which keeps the record (/var/lib/nex/image/state.json). The result says only whether the engine accepted the request (apply, activate, rollback and cancel start or settle work in the background); a refusal is a failed result whose error is "<code>: <message>" with the engine's stable code (for example update_in_progress, nothing_staged, already_armed, state_format_downgrade). request_id is the engine's idempotency key, so a redelivered command replays the original operation. Nothing is pool-scoped and no pool rollout gate is evaluated. Sent only to a host that offered image-update-v1.

host-system-disk-replace.semantics: Addressed to one host and performed entirely by its own Core, which keeps the record (<agent state dir>/system-disk/replace.json) and runs the replacement on a goroutine of its own, so it outlives the command, the Controller connection and a restart of Core. Core revalidates the selected disk against a fresh disk observation (identity, fingerprint, eligibility, the typed erase confirmation), refuses the disk the running system started from and any disk that holds data without that confirmation, then lays the surviving disk's partition table on the replacement, copies the surviving disk's verified slots (verity-checked before and after the copy), formats and fills the boot partition through the host's boot method (shim, signed GRUB and a firmware boot entry on UEFI, GRUB with grub-install on BIOS) and adds the replacement's nex-data partition to the md mirror with mdadm --add. The result is succeeded when the member was added (the kernel resyncs in the background and reports it), failed with Core's own sentence when it refused or failed, or needs_attention with a still_running text when the replacement outlived the 5 minute wait of the host's worker; the host's record (system_disk in the hardware report) is the truth. request_id is the idempotency key: the same request replays its recorded outcome, another request for the same disk continues an interrupted or failed replacement, and a request for another disk while one runs is refused unless the running one's disk is no longer reported at all, in which case that replacement is recorded as failed and the new one starts. Sent only to a host that offered host-system-disk-replace-v1.

pool-update.semantics: Addressed to the pool master. PoolCommand.action is update-rollout (start, or with update.dry_run a preflight only) or update-control (update.control pause, resume, abort or rollback_host with update.rollout_id and, for rollback_host, update.host_id); membership carries only master_host_id. The master's coordinator owns the multi-step job and its durable record (pool-update.json, replicated as the authority section update_rollout); the result says only whether the master accepted the request: succeeded, or failed with "<code>: <message>". request_id is the rollout ID, so a redelivered command returns the rollout it already made. Capability pool-update-rollout-v1; the Controller sends it only when the master and every member advertise it.

backup-orphan-cleanup.semantics: Controller queues deletion of chosen missing VMs' recovery points from a repository on the pool master. Core re-checks at execution that each VM is still absent from its durable VM inventory and that the point counts match the confirmed ones, else fails the Result deleting nothing. It records the plan and per-point outcomes on the master, then deletes each point's destination data and catalog entry through the retention delete. Protected points are skipped unless include_protected; points pinned by an unfinished restore or test restore, named by a pending run, or whose VM exists again are skipped. A repeated or interrupted command continues from the recorded plan; replays by request_id return the recorded Result.

vm-release-retained.semantics: Delete the disk files and vTPM state that restore replace and VM edits retained for a managed VM. Requires observed shut off, confirmation equal to the VM name, no retained snapshots and no unfinished VM or restore operation; files in the current disk chain are never removed and each file is checked like a vm-delete wipe (registered storage directory, regular file, no other domain uses it). The journal on the VM's host records the released paths, so an exact replay returns the recorded result and an interrupted release re-runs, skipping files already gone. Released paths stop counting as storage-detach dependencies.
